notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Numbers 33:29–56, drawn from the sources available:

---

## Numbers 33:29–56 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 29 — "They set out from Mithkah and camped at Hashmonah."

**Name Meanings and Location:** Several sources suggest possible meanings of these place-names. Mithkah may mean "Sweetness" and Hashmonah "Swiftness." The site of Hashmonah is possibly the same as Heshmon in Joshua 15:27, a town in the territory of Judah. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Gill** computes the distance from Mithkah to Hashmonah at about eight miles, noting that all these stations in the central section (vv. 19–29) are otherwise unknown and recorded nowhere else in Scripture. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 30 — "They set out from Hashmonah and camped at Moseroth."

**Connection to Deuteronomy 10:6:** Moseroth is the plural form of Mosera, mentioned in Deuteronomy 10:6 as the place where Aaron died. This is one of the few place-names in this section that appears elsewhere in Scripture. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

**Whedon** notes that Hengstenberg thought Moseroth lay in the Arabah where Mount Hor overhangs it, and Burckhardt suggested Wady Mousa near Petra preserves the name. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-33.html)

**Gill** calculates the distance from Hashmonah to Moseroth at thirty-two miles. He notes the apparent discrepancy with Deuteronomy 10:6 (where they went from Bene-jaakan to Mosera) and suggests the Israelites went back and forth between these places. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 31 — "They set out from Moseroth and camped at Bene-jaakan."

**Full Name:** The full name in Deuteronomy 10:6 is Beeroth-bene-Jaakan, "the wells of the children of Jaakan." Jaakan (or Akan) was a grandson of Seir, the legendary father of the Horites of Mount Seir (Genesis 36:20, 27; 1 Chronicles 1:42). The wells may have retained the name long after the original owners were dispossessed. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-31.htm)

**Keil & Delitzsch** suggest the wells of Jaakan should be sought on the mountains that bound the Arabah on either the east or west. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 32 — "They set out from Bene-jaakan and camped at Hor-haggidgad."

**Name Meaning:** Hor-haggidgad means "the Hollow of Gidgad" or "cave of Gidgad." In Deuteronomy 10:7 it appears as Gudgodah, which is a slightly altered and abbreviated form. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch** note that Gudgodah may have been the unnamed encampment of Numbers 21:4 where the people were punished with fiery serpents. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 33 — "They set out from Hor-haggidgad and camped at Jotbathah."

**Meaning and Character:** Jotbathah means "Pleasantness." Deuteronomy 10:7 describes it as "a land of water-brooks," suggesting it was a green oasis with streams flowing through it in the midst of the arid Arabah steppe. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch** place Jotbathah before Zalmonah (v. 41) and note that nothing of importance occurred here, hence its omission in the historical narrative of Numbers 20–21. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 34 — "They set out from Jotbathah and camped at Abronah."

**Name Meaning:** Abronah means "Regions Beyond" or "Passage." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

Beyond the name and its location somewhere in the Arabah on the route south toward the Red Sea, the commentators treat Abronah as one of the many stations about which nothing further is known. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 35 — "They set out from Abronah and camped at Ezion-geber."

**A Known Location:** Ezion-geber is the one location in the list of seventeen (vv. 19–36) that can be identified with certainty. It was the well-known port at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba (the Elanitic Gulf), where Solomon and Jehoshaphat later built fleets to sail to Ophir (1 Kings 9:26; 22:48). It was near Elath (modern Aqaba). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

**Name Meaning:** "Mighty Trees" or possibly "Backbone of a Mighty One." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

---

### v. 36 — "They set out from Ezion-geber and camped at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin."

**A Major Turning Point:** Kadesh (Kadesh-barnea) was the place from which the twelve spies were sent out (Numbers 13). The Wilderness of Zin is distinguished from the Wilderness of Sin (v. 11). This encampment marks the end of the long thirty-seven years of wandering and a return to the border of Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Gill** computes the distance from Ezion-geber to Kadesh as forty-eight miles. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

**Keil & Delitzsch** frame vv. 19–36 as covering the 37 years of wandering that followed the refusal to enter Canaan, with Kadesh representing the point where the new generation again stood at the threshold. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary)

---

### v. 37 — "They set out from Kadesh and camped at Mount Hor, on the outskirts of the land of Edom."

**Mount Hor and Edom:** Mount Hor lay on the border of Edom. It was here that Aaron died. The Israelites attempted to enter Canaan by this route but were repulsed by the king of Arad (v. 40). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-33.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch** note that Numbers 20:23 and Deuteronomy 10:6 both place Aaron's death at this location, though Deuteronomy 10:6 mentions Mosera as the encampment from which he went up. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 38 — "At the LORD’s command, Aaron the priest climbed Mount Hor and died there on the first day of the fifth month, in the fortieth year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt."

**Obedience in Death:** Multiple commentators note the significance that Aaron "went up at the command of the LORD and died." It was an act of obedience — "a good way to go home by obeying the last command." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary)

**The Date:** This is the only place in Scripture where the exact date of Aaron's death is given: the first day of the fifth month (the month Ab, corresponding to part of July/August). He died just four months after his sister Miriam (Numbers 20:1). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-38.htm)

**The Fortieth Year:** The timing accords with God's decree that Israel would wander forty years (Numbers 14:33–34), "that period being understood, according to the usual mercy of God, which shortens the days of evil, to include the time already spent in the wilderness." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/33.htm)

**Calvin** notes that Aaron's life was "prolonged to an unusual period, for the good of the people," making Israel's ingratitude "the more base in not acknowledging this paternal care of God." (https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol06/htm/ii.xxvi.htm)

**Sailhamer** observes that within the list of encampments, two short narratives focus on Moses (v. 2) and Aaron (vv. 38–39), both obeying "the command of the LORD," giving a brief review of these two great leaders' work. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/33-38.html)

---

### v. 39 — "Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor."

**A Mark of Blessing:** Ronald Allen comments that Aaron's "death came at a great age — a mark of God's blessing in his life. By the mercy of the Lord, his time was extended to the very last year of Israel's desert experience; his own sin (Numbers 20) kept him from living into the time of the conquest of the land." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-33-commentary)

**Age Comparison:** Aaron was three years older than his brother Moses. He was eighty-three when he stood before Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7), and the forty years since then bring the total to 123. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 40 — "Now the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev in the land of Canaan, heard that the Israelites were coming."

**A Parenthetical Notice:** This fragmentary notice about king Arad is understood as a parenthesis. The fuller account appears in Numbers 21:1–3, where the king of Arad fought against Israel and took some captives, after which Israel vowed to destroy his cities. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/numbers-33.html)

**Gill** adds that this occurred while Israel was at Mount Hor. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 41 — "And the Israelites set out from Mount Hor and camped at Zalmonah."

**Name Meaning:** Zalmonah may mean "Resemblance" or "Image." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Possible Location of the Fiery Serpents:** Some traditions (noted in the Haydock Catholic Commentary) think Zalmonah is where God sent the fiery serpents (Numbers 21:6), though the biblical text does not explicitly state this. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 42 — "They set out from Zalmonah and camped at Punon."

Punon is one of the stations whose location and meaning remain unknown. It appears only here in the itinerary. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

---

### v. 43 — "They set out from Punon and camped at Oboth."

**Name Meaning:** Oboth means "Water Skins," perhaps indicating a place where water was carried or stored. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Gill** computes the distance from Punon to Oboth as twenty-four miles. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 44 — "They set out from Oboth and camped at Iye-abarim on the border of Moab."

**Name Meaning:** Iye-abarim (or Ije-abarim) means "The Heaps (or Ruins) of Abarim." It lay on the border of Moab, marking Israel's approach to the territories east of the Jordan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Gill** gives the distance from Oboth as sixteen miles. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 45 — "They set out from Iyim and camped at Dibon-gad."

**Name Meaning:** Dibon-gad means "Built Up by Gad." The name likely reflects the fact that the tribe of Gad later rebuilt or occupied this city (Numbers 32:34). The shortened form "Iyim" in this verse is the same as Iye-abarim or Ijim of the previous verse. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

**Haydock** notes that Dibon was on the border between the territories of Reuben and Gad. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 46 — "They set out from Dibon-gad and camped at Almon-diblathaim."

**Name Meaning:** Almon-diblathaim may mean "Hidden Figs" or "Concealed Fig-Cakes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Gill** notes it may be the same as Diblath in Ezekiel 6:14. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 47 — "They set out from Almon-diblathaim and camped in the mountains of Abarim facing Nebo."

**The Mountains of Abarim:** Abarim means "The Mountains Beyond" (i.e., beyond the Jordan). They face Nebo, which is the mountain from which Moses would later view the Promised Land and die (Deuteronomy 34:1). This is the last station before the plains of Moab. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

---

### v. 48 — "They set out from the mountains of Abarim and camped on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho."

**The Final Encampment:** This is the place where Israel now found itself — the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho. It is here that the remaining events of Numbers, the whole of Deuteronomy, and the final preparations for entering Canaan take place. All the events involving Balak and Balaam (Numbers 22–24) occurred while Israel was encamped here. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 49 — "And there on the plains of Moab they camped by the Jordan, from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim."

**Extent of the Camp:** The camp stretched from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim (also called simply Shittim), a distance of over five miles (some Jewish sources say twelve miles), suitable for the vast numbers of Israel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Abel-shittim:** The name includes "Abel," meaning "mourning," which the Targum connects to the mourning over the plague in which 24,000 died (Numbers 25:1–9). The "shittim" (acacia) trees grew in the area. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

---

### v. 50 — "On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, the LORD said to Moses…"

**A New Section Begins:** Keil & Delitzsch emphasize that this introductory formula marks the beginning of a new legal section (vv. 50–56) that serves as "the general legal foundation for the more minute instructions in Numbers 34–36." It is not merely an appendix to the travel list but the opening of commands concerning the conquest and settlement. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 51 — "Speak to the Israelites and tell them: When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan…"

This verse sets the context: the command looks forward to the seventh and final stage — crossing the Jordan into Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

---

### v. 52 — "…you must drive out before you all the inhabitants of the land, destroy all their carved images and cast idols, and demolish all their high places."

**Four Hebrew Verbs:** David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/Pentecostal tradition) notes that four different Hebrew verbs are used (translated *drive out*, *destroy*, *destroy*, and *demolish*), expressing the totality of what was commanded — nothing of Canaanite idolatrous culture was to remain. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (Reformed/Presbyterian):** "Drive out" means not merely expulsion but extermination (see Deuteronomy 7:1). "Pictures" (KJV) are understood as obelisks for idolatrous worship (see Leviticus 26:1). "High places" refers by metonymy to all groves, altars, and materials of worship on hilltops. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/33.htm)

**Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** *Maskith* = an idol of stone (cf. Leviticus 26:1); *massecah* = idols cast from brass (see Exodus 32:4); *bamoth* = altars of the Canaanites upon high places (see Leviticus 26:30). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

**Whedon (Methodist):** Clarifies that "pictures" (KJV) is literally "idols of stone" (RV "figured stones"). He adds: "This verse is not to be construed as a charter for universal iconoclasm. In the case of Israel, strongly inclined to idolatry, this was the only safe course." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-33.html)

**Morgan (interdenominational):** "No false pity or selfish motive was to operate in such fashion as to leave any corrupting influence behind. The unequivocal command to drive out all, was based on the tenderest regard of God for the well-being of the chosen people, and through them, the whole human race." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

**Haydock (Catholic):** Notes the Hebrew refers to "stones placed on high to be seen" and the Septuagint renders it "towers of the sentinels"; the Chaldean paraphrase has "temples where they adore their idols." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-33.html)

**Ronald Allen (Evangelical):** "Pluralism in the form of peaceful coexistence with idolatry would be impossible, both for the well-being of the people and the sanctity of the land Yahweh had given as a gift to his people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

---

### v. 53 — "You are to take possession of the land and settle in it, for I have given you the land to possess."

**The Divine Gift:** The land is a gift from Yahweh. The Hebrew verb *yarash* means both "to take possession of" and "to drive out" — the positive and negative sides of the same command. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

**Calvin (Reformed) on the connection between vv. 52–53:** "God declares connectedly, 'Ye shall dispossess the inhabitants of the land, and dwell therein, for I have given you the land to possess it' — it would have been absurd that one clause should be disjoined from the other." The dispossession and possession belong together as one divine act. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/33-50.html)

---

### v. 54 — "And you are to divide the land by lot according to your clans. Give a larger inheritance to a larger clan and a smaller inheritance to a smaller one. Whatever falls to each one by lot will be his. You will receive an inheritance according to the tribes of your fathers."

**Repetition from Numbers 26:** This is substantially a verbal repetition of Numbers 26:53–56. The particular location of each tribe was determined by lot, but the size of the inheritance was proportionate to the size of the tribe. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/33.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-33.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch** explain the Hebrew idiom: "into that, whither the lot comes out to him, shall be to him" — i.e., each family receives the portion to which the lot points. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

**The Pulpit Commentary** adds: "Not only the tribe, but the family and the household, was to receive its special inheritance by lot; no doubt in such a way that the final settlement of the country would correspond with the blood relationships of the settlers." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-33.html)

---

### v. 55 — "But if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land before you, those you allow to remain will become barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides; they will harass you in the land where you settle."

**A New Warning:** This solemn warning appears here for the first time. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the call for it "had been furnished by their past transgressions in the matter of Baal-peor, and by their imperfect fulfillment, at the first, of Moses' orders in the Midianite war." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/33-56.htm)

**The Imagery:** "Pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides" — natural symbols of dangerous and painful annoyances. The Pulpit Commentary suggests "possibly the thickets which fringe the Jordan supplied them with present examples." Joshua 23:13 later flips the imagery to "scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-33.html)

**Adam Clarke (Methodist):** "Under these metaphors, the continual mischief that should be done to them, both in soul and body, by these idolaters, is set forth in a very expressive manner. What can be more vexatious than a continual goading of each side, so that the attempt to avoid the one throws the body more forcibly on the other? And what can be more distressing than a continual pricking in the eye, harassing the mind, tormenting the body, and extinguishing the sight?" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/numbers-33.html)

**Matthew Henry (via the Biblical Illustrator):** "That which we are willing should tempt us we shall find will vex us." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/numbers-33.html)

**Gill (Baptist/Reformed Baptist):** These figurative expressions "show that they should be very troublesome and distressing to them, even in their most tender and nearest concerns, and dearest relations… drawing them into sin through their ill examples, and so bring the displeasure of God upon them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

**Sadly Prophetic:** Allen notes, "The description of trouble is, of course, sadly prophetic," fulfilled in Judges and throughout Israel's subsequent history. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

---

### v. 56 — "And then I will do to you what I had planned to do to them."

**The Ultimate Threat:** God is no respecter of persons or nations. If Israel behaved like the Canaanites, they would suffer the Canaanites' fate. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-33.html)

**Ellicott (Anglican):** "It must be borne in mind that the idolatrous inhabitants of Canaan were never wholly exterminated, and the pernicious influence which they exercised was felt throughout the whole of the history of the Israelites until the judgments threatened against them were finally executed in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers-33.htm)

**Benson (Methodist):** "Make you their slaves; or rather, you shall flee before them, and be expelled the land, as they should have been." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/numbers-33.html)

**Spiritual Application — JFB (Reformed/Presbyterian):** "This earnest admonition given to the Israelites in their peculiar circumstances conveys a salutary lesson to us to allow no lurking habits of sin to remain in us. That spiritual enemy must be eradicated from our nature; otherwise it will be ruinous to our present peace and future salvation." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/33.htm)

**Spiritual Application — Matthew Henry (via StudyLight):** "If we do not drive sin out, sin will drive us out; if we be not the death of our lusts, our lusts will be the death of our souls." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/33-56.html)

**The Pulpit Commentary** addresses the moral difficulty of the extermination command: "The command to extirpate was certainly justified in this case (if it could be in any) by the unhappy consequences of its neglect. Israel being what he was, and so little severed in anything but religion from the ancient heathen, his only chance of future happiness lay in keeping himself from any contact with them." It adds that the command "was not contrary to the moral law as then revealed, or to the moral sense as then educated." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/numbers-33.html)

**Haydock (Catholic):** Notes that God made use of the remaining Canaanites "to scourge his people, and to train them for war" (Du Hamel), and that the Israelites "proved negligent" in carrying out the command. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-33.html)

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Other Views

### On the Command to Drive Out / Destroy (vv. 52–53, 55–56)

- **Reformed / Presbyterian (JFB, Calvin):** Stress the completeness of the command as divine judgment on Canaanite sin. Calvin connects dispossession and possession as one act of God's sovereignty. JFB draws the spiritual lesson about eradicating sin in the believer's life. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/numbers/33.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/33-50.html)

- **Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** Treat the passage as legal foundation for Numbers 34–36, with careful attention to Hebrew vocabulary and the structure of the section. No significant doctrinal divergence from other conservative Protestant readings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/numbers-33.html)

- **Methodist / Wesleyan (Whedon, Benson, Clarke):** Whedon explicitly limits the application: "This verse is not to be construed as a charter for universal iconoclasm." Clarke vividly expands on the "pricks in your eyes" metaphor. Benson applies the threat historically to Israel's exile. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-33.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/numbers-33.html)

- **Baptist (Gill):** Gill focuses on the exegetical details (distances, name meanings) and the historical fulfillment in Israel's later captivities. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary touches on the connection to Deuteronomy 10:6. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-33.html)

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasizes the four Hebrew verbs for the totality of the command and the spiritual principle for the church: "It is of no use for the church to succeed in the eyes of man… if it merely allows the corrupt practices and attitudes of the Canaanites to take root among God's people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott notes the historical outworking — the Canaanites were never fully exterminated, and the threat in v. 56 was fulfilled in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/33.htm)

- **Catholic (Haydock):** Haydock follows the traditional Catholic reading with reference to the Septuagint, Chaldean paraphrase, and Fathers. He notes that these stations were understood typologically by the Fathers as "steps and degrees by which Christians, leaving sin, are to advance from virtue to virtue." On v. 55, he draws from Calmet: the abandoned nations "must not be spared through a false pity." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-33.html)

- **Modern Scholarship / NET Bible notes:** Not directly retrieved for this passage. However, Enduring Word mentions the NET Bible rendering of v. 2 ("Moses recorded their departures according to their journeys"), and notes the scholarly view that the list is presented in the style of ancient Near Eastern kings' conquest records — Yahweh's victory procession. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

- **Orthodox (OCA):** No specific Orthodox commentary on this passage was retrieved from the permitted sites.

---

### On Allegorical / Spiritual Readings of the Journey List

- **Haydock (Catholic):** The 42 stations were understood by the Church Fathers as figures of the soul's progress from sin to the heavenly mansions. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-33.html)

- **Gill (Baptist):** Cautions against over-allegorizing, noting that "though the travels of the children of Israel in the wilderness may in general be an emblem of the case and condition of the people of God in this world… the particulars will never hold good of individual saints, since they are not all led exactly in the same path." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/33.htm)

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** While listing possible name meanings, Guzik cites Clarke's warning: "In cases of this kind fancy has much more to do than judgment." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-33/)

---

*Note: No material on specifically "prosperity," "Word of Faith," or "hyper-grace" interpretations of this passage was found in the permitted sources.*
